**Understanding the problem**
Each worker (skill w) can do at most one task, and only a task whose requirement equals their skill exactly. One extra universal worker can do any single task. Maximize total profit.

**Examples:** Example 1: skills 1..5; tasks (1,100),(2,400),(3,100),(3,400). Matched workers earn 100+400+400, the extra worker takes the remaining (3,100) → 1000. Example 2: no worker has skill 1, so only the extra worker works → 100. Example 3: worker skill 7 matches nothing; extra worker takes one (3,3) → 3.

With n up to 10⁵ we need a linearithmic greedy, not exhaustive matching.
k: Workers whose skill matches no task are useless; matched workers should each take the highest-profit task of their exact skill.
Process tasks in decreasing profit order: assign to an idle matching worker if one exists, otherwise the task becomes a leftover candidate.
The universal worker takes the single most profitable leftover task.

a.i: Sorting tasks by profit descending and greedily assigning each to an unused worker with exactly matching skill is optimal: any solution can be exchanged so that a matched worker takes the best available task of its skill without loss. Tasks that no matched worker can take compete only for the universal worker, who should take the largest among them.
s: Put worker skills into a set.
Scan tasks: if an idle worker has the required skill, assign (add profit, remove skill); otherwise record the profit as a leftover.
Add the maximum leftover profit (0 if none) to the total.
a.t: O(T log T + W) — sorting tasks dominates; the scan and set operations are linear/amortized O(1).
a.sp: O(W) — the set of available skills.

w:
**Wrap-up**
Present the sort-and-greedy; a heap-per-skill variant (pop the top profit of each matched worker's skill, then take the max remaining across skills for the extra worker) achieves the same result with more code. Pitfalls: forgetting the universal worker when nothing matches (example 3); using ≥ instead of exact skill equality; 32-bit overflow of the profit sum (up to 10⁵ × 10⁹) — use 64-bit. Follow-up: what if each worker could do k tasks, or the extra worker had a limited skill range?
